title: Phrasal verbs
intro: Phrasal verbs are everywhere in English. Learn how they work, how to place the object and the most useful verbs by topic. The B2 part adds more meanings and style.

sections.title: What are phrasal verbs?
sections.summary: A phrasal verb is a verb plus a small word (a particle) with a meaning that is often different from the parts.

tables.caption: Four types of phrasal verb
head: type
rule
example
rows: The plane took off. Please sit down.
verb + object + particle, or verb + particle + object
Turn off the light. Turn the light off.
the object stays after the particle
Look after the baby. Look after her.
We ran out of milk. I look forward to it.

uses: The meaning often cannot be guessed: give up = stop; put off = delay.
Many phrasal verbs have more than one meaning: take off is for planes, and also for clothes.
They are common in speaking and informal writing. In formal writing you can use a single verb: continue instead of go on.
Learn the whole phrase and an example, not only the particle.

examples.text: She gave up smoking last year.
The meeting has been put off until Friday.
I am looking forward to the holidays.

mistakes.why: A pronoun object goes between the verb and the particle.

checks.question: Rewrite with it: Turn off the TV.
checks.explanation: With a separable verb a pronoun goes in the middle.

checks.question: Choose: We ran (out of / out) money.

sections.title: Separable and inseparable
sections.summary: Check whether the object can stand between the verb and the particle.

tables.caption: Position of the object
head: verb
noun object
pronoun object
rows: turn on the radio / turn the radio on
fill in the form / fill the form in
take off your coat / take your coat off

uses: With a noun object, separable verbs can go in two ways. With a pronoun they must be split.
A long object usually goes after the particle: Put on the black jacket that you bought.
Inseparable verbs and three-part verbs never split.
A dictionary shows [T] for separable verbs and [I] for verbs with no object.

examples.text: Switch the light off when you leave. Switch it off.

examples.note: Called the match off is also possible.

checks.question: Rewrite with them: Put away the books.
checks.explanation: A pronoun goes in the middle.

checks.question: Rewrite with her: I look after my sister.

sections.title: Common phrasal verbs by topic
sections.summary: Group phrasal verbs by topic or by particle to learn them faster.

tables.caption: Everyday phrasal verbs
head: topic
phrasal verb
meaning
rows: register at a hotel or airport
enter or leave a bus, train or plane
search in a book or online
stop trying or stop a habit

uses: Learn each verb with one example sentence that you can say about your own life.
The same particle often gives a similar idea: up = increase or finish (use up, eat up), off = start a journey or remove, out = leave or discover.
Check the Cambridge vocabulary list: the entries marked phr v are the phrasal verbs of the B1 exam.

examples.text: We set off at six to avoid the traffic.
I looked the word up in a dictionary.

mistakes.wrong: I will wake up you at seven.
mistakes.right: I will wake you up at seven.
mistakes.why: A pronoun or short object splits the verb.
Run out of is a three-part verb.

checks.question: Complete: Please ___ the form in capitals. (fill + particle)
Complete: I need to ___ my keys. I can't find them. (look + particle)

sections.title: More phrasal verbs, meanings and style
sections.summary: At B2 you meet more abstract meanings, verbs with more than one meaning and the difference between formal and informal.

tables.caption: Phrasal verbs and formal verbs
head: informal phrasal verb
formal verb
example
rows: They put off the wedding. / They postponed the wedding.
He came up with a plan.

uses: One phrasal verb can have several meanings: pick up = lift, learn quickly, collect, improve.
Use the context and the particle to guess meanings you do not know.
Choose a single verb in formal writing such as an essay, a report or an application.
Be careful with literal and idiomatic uses: take off the hat (literal), the business took off (became successful).

examples.text: She picked up Spanish very quickly.
The company came up with a new idea.
He brought up the problem at the meeting.

mistakes.wrong: The match was called out because of rain.
mistakes.right: The match was called off because of rain.

mistakes.wrong: I came with a good idea.
mistakes.right: I came up with a good idea.
mistakes.why: Come up with is a three-part verb.

checks.question: Rewrite in a formal style: We put off the meeting.
checks.explanation: Postpone is the formal verb for put off.

checks.question: Complete: She ___ her children alone. (bring + particle)
